'''Scott Frederick Gilbert''' (born 1949) is an American [[evolutionary developmental biology|evolutionary developmental biologist]] and historian of biology.

Scott Gilbert is the Howard A. Schneiderman Professor of Biology (''emeritus'') at [[Swarthmore College]] and a Finland Distinguished Professor (''emeritus'') at the [[University of Helsinki]].

== Education ==
He obtained his B.A. in both biology and religion from [[Wesleyan University]] (1971). In 1976, he received his MA (history of science, under the aegis of [[Donna Haraway]]) and his PhD (biology, in the laboratory of [[Barbara Migeon]]) from the [[Johns Hopkins University]].<ref name="auto">Gilbert S. F. 2009. Bio. ''Evolution and Development'' 11: 331 – 332.</ref> His postdoctoral work at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]], pursued research on ribosome synthesis in the laboratory of [[Masayasu Nomura]] (1976–1978) and investigated developmental immunology in the laboratory of [[Robert Auerbach]] (1978–1980).<ref name="auto"/>

== Academic career ==
Gilbert is the author of the textbook ''Developmental Biology'' (first edition, 1985, and now in its 13th edition, 2023) and has also co-authored (with [[David Epel]]) the textbook ''Ecological Developmental Biology'' (2009, 2015). He has been credited with helping initiate [[evolutionary developmental biology]] and ecological developmental biology as new biological disciplines.<ref>Mikhailov, A. T. and Gilbert S. F. 2005. Putting evo-devo into focus: An interview with Scott F. Gilbert. ''International Journal of Developmental Biology'' 48: 9 – 16.</ref><ref name="auto1">Gilbert, S. F. 2001. Ecological developmental biology: Developmental biology meets the real world. ''Developmental Biology '' 233: 1 - 12.</ref><ref>Duschek, J. It's the ecology, stupid. ''Nature'' 418: 578 - 579.</ref><ref>Wake, M., Development in the real world. Reviewed Work: ''Ecological Developmental Biology: Integrating Epigenetics, Medicine, and Evolution'' by Scott F. Gilbert, David Epel. ''Amer. Sci.'' 98(1): 75-78.</ref>

Gilbert's early biological research includes documenting the first [[pyrimidine]]-initiated RNA transcripts,<ref>Gilbert, S. F., Boer, H. A. de, and Nomura, M. 1979. Identification of initiation sites for the ''in vitro'' transcription of rRNA operons ''rrnE'' and ''rrnA'' in ''Escherichia  coli.''  ''Cell'' 17: 211-224.</ref> elucidating the mechanisms by which antibodies inactivate [[poliovirus]],<ref>Icenogle, J., Shiwen, H., Duke, G., Gilbert, S. F., Rueckert, R., and Anderegg, J. 1983. Neutralization of poliovirus by a monoclonal antibody:  Kinetics and stoichiometry. ''Virology'' 127: 412 - 425.</ref> and studying the roles of paracrine factors in kidney and lung branching.<ref>Cebra-Thomas, J. A., Bromer, J., Gardner, R., Lam, G. K., Scheipe, H., and Gilbert, S. F.  2003. ''T-box'' gene products are required for mesenchymal induction of epithelial branching in the embryonic mouse lung. ''Developmental Dynamics226'': 82 - 90.</ref><ref>Ritvos, O., Tuuri, T., Erämaa, M., Sainio, K., Hilden, K., Saxén, L., and Gilbert, S. F.  1995. Activin disrupts epithelial branching morphogenesis in developing murine kidney, pancreas, and salivary gland. ''Mechanisms of Development '' 50: 229 - 245.</ref> After co-authoring an early paper in evolutionary developmental biology,<ref>Gilbert, S. F., Opitz, J., and Raff, R. A. 1996. Resynthesizing evolutionary and developmental biology. ''Developmental Biology'' 173: 357 - 372.</ref> he inaugurated a project on the development of turtle  shells. With collaborator [[Judith Cebra-Thomas]], Gilbert elucidated the roles of several paracrine factors involved in [[carapace]] formation and made the unexpected conclusion that the [[plastron]] was derived from [[Truncal neural crest|trunk neural crest]] cells. The latter studies led to the hypothesis that the turtle evolved by respecifying its cell types.<ref>Gilbert, S. F., Cebra-Thomas, J. A., and Burke, A. C. (2007). How the turtle gets its shell. In ''Biology of Turtles'' (J. Wyneken, M. H. Gofrey, and V. Bels, eds.). CRC Press, Boca Raton. Pp. 1- 16.</ref><ref>Cebra-Thomas, J. A., Betters, E., Yin, M., Plafkin, C., McDow, K., and Gilbert, S. F. 2007. A late-emerging population of trunk neural crest cells forms the plastron in the turtle ''Trachemys scripta''. ''Evolution and Development'' 9: 267 – 277''.''</ref> His most recent studies concern the development of the [[holobiont]] and the importance of [[Phenotypic plasticity|plasticity]] and symbiotic microbes during normal animal development.<ref>Gilbert, S.F., Sapp. J., and Tauber, A. I. 2012. A symbiotic view of life: We have never been individuals. ''Quarterly Review of Biology'' 87: 325 – 341.</ref><ref>Gilbert, Scott F; Bosch, Thomas C. G; Ledón-Rettig, Cristina. (2015). "Eco-Evo-Devo: developmental symbiosis and developmental plasticity as evolutionary agents". ''[[Nature Reviews Genetics]]'' 16: 611–622.</ref> He has argued that the holobiont is an important unit of [[evolutionary selection]].<ref>Roughgarden, J., Gilbert, S. F., Rosenberg, E., Zilber-Rosenberg, I, and Lloyd, E. A. 2017. Holobionts as units of selection and a model of their population dynamics and evolution. ''Biological Theory'' 13: ''44-65.''</ref>

Gilbert's research in the history and philosophy of biology concerns the interactions of [[genetics]] and [[embryology]]; feminist critiques of biology; [[Antireductionism]]; the formation of biological disciplines; and [[Bioethics]]. Some of these studies have documented the origins of the gene theory from embryological controversies,<ref>Gilbert, S. F. 1978.  The embryological origins of the gene theory. ''J. Hist. Biol.'' 11: 307-351.</ref><ref>Gilbert, S. F. 1988.  Cellular Politics:  Just, Goldschmidt, and the attempts to reconcile embryology and genetics,  In ''The American Development of Biology''  (ed. R. Rainger, K. Benson, J. Maienschein) University of Pennsylvania Press, Philadelphia. pp. 311-346.</ref> the formation of [[molecular biology]] and [[biochemistry]] as separate disciplines,<ref>Gilbert, S. F. 1982.  Intellectual traditions in the life sciences:  Molecular biology and biochemistry.  ''Perspec. Biol. Med''. 26: 151-162.</ref> the importance of feminist critique as a normative control in cell and developmental biology,<ref>Beldecos, A., Bailly, S., Gilbert, S., Hicks, K., Kenschaft, L., Niemczyk, N., Rosenberg, R., Schaertel, S., and Wedel, A. 1988.  The importance of feminist critique for contemporary cell biology.  ''Hypatia'' 3:  61-76.</ref><ref>Gilbert, S. F. and Howes-Mischel 2004. "Show Me Your Original Face before You Were Born": The Convergence of Public Fetuses and Sacred DNA. ''History and Philosophy of the Life Sciences'' 26: 377 – 394.</ref> and the importance of the environment in [[phenotype]] production.<ref name="auto1"/><ref>Gilbert, S. F. 2012. Ecological developmental biology: Environmental signals for normal animal development. ''Evolution and Development'' 14: 20 – 28.</ref><ref>Gilbert, S. F. 2002. Genetic determinism: The battle between scientific data and social image in contemporary developmental biology. In ''On Human Nature. Anthropological, Biological, and Philosophical Foundations''. (Grunwald, A., Gutmann, M., and Neumann-Held, E. M., eds.) Springer-Verlag, NY. Pp. 121 - 140.</ref> His work in the interactions of biology and religion have included extensive analysis of wonder,<ref>Gilbert, S. F. 2013. Wonder and the necessary alliances of science and religion''. Euresis Journal'' 4: 7-30.</ref> as well as studies of when different groups of biologists claim that individual human life begins.<ref>Gilbert, S. F. 2008. When "personhood" begins in the embryo: avoiding a syllabus of errors. ''Birth Defects Res C Embryo Today'' 84: 164 - 173.</ref> He has identified (with [[Ziony Zevit]]) the bone from which Eve was generated,<ref>Gilbert, S. F. and Zevit, Z. 2001. Congenital human baculum deficiency: The generative bone of ''Genesis'' 2: 21-23. ''American Journal of Medical Genetics'' 101: 284 - 285.</ref> analyzed embryonic imagery in the art of [[Gustav Klimt]], [[Diego Rivera]], and [[Frida Kahlo]],<ref>Gilbert. S. F. and Braukmann, S. 2011. Fertilization narratives in the art of Gustav Klimt, Diego Rivera, and Frida Kahlo: Repression, Domination, and Eros among cells. ''Leonardo'' 44: 221 – 227.</ref> and has provided one of the first analyses of [[nerd humor]].<ref>Gilbert, S. F. 1985.  Bacchus in the laboratory:  In defense of scientific puns. ''Perspec. Biol. Med''. 29: 148-152.</ref> His biology textbooks have been experiments in the interactions between biology and its social critiques.

Gilbert is frequently invited to lecture on this subject and has given this talk to diverse audiences from around the country to the Vatican. This lecture was recorded at the annual conference sponsored by the Association of Reproductive Health Professionals, Planned Parenthood of America, and the Society of Family Planning.<ref>Swarthmore. When Does Personhood Begin?. https://www.swarthmore.edu/news-events/when-does-personhood-begin</ref> His commitment to sexual and reproductive rights is evident in the article he wrote for San Francisco Chronicle, in which at the end he asks to support Planned Parenthood.<ref>Gilbert. S. April, 11 2017. To stop abortions, protect the EPA, don’t attack Planned Parenthood. San Francisco Chronicle. https://perma-archives.org/warc/20171018171021/http://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/To-stop-abortions-protect-the-EPA-don-t-11066734.php</ref>

== Personal life ==
Scott F. Gilbert is the son of Marvin (Bud) and Elaine Caplan Gilbert. He was raised in [[East Rockaway, New York]], .<ref name="auto"/> He is married to [[Anne Raunio]] (m.1971), and has three children and two grandchildren. In 2015, Gilbert became emeritus professor at both Swarthmore College and the University of Helsinki, and in 2016 he moved with Anne to Portland, Oregon, where he is on the Asian Arts Council of the [[Portland Art Museum]].
